item.title: ORC Assignment 1: Arranging for Band
item.dc:creator: Pedro
item.description: I had a lot of fun with this arrangement. I chose American Pie because it’s a recognisable tune that works both slow and mellow and fast and rhythmic, so I went for a mixture of the two....
item.content:encoded:
I had a lot of fun with this arrangement. I chose American Pie because it’s a recognisable tune that works both slow and mellow and fast and rhythmic, so I went for a mixture of the two. I also picked it because I grew up watching American college brass bands, so my mind went straight to American songs.

The song is longer than the two minutes allowed, so I chose a slow opening verse, followed by a more jolly and cheerful chorus, a verse, and a final chorus with a modulation.

Transposition was a challenge. I first wrote the arrangement in B♭, the usual brass band key, but I wanted to keep the song’s original key of G. It simply sounded better, or perhaps I’m just used to hearing it at that pitch. I also had to keep checking ranges. For example, I moved a euphonium run down an octave because it had become too high.

Shaping the texture was another challenge. I contrasted a solo flugelhorn introduction and a verse led by the euphonium with full-band choruses, and I modulated up a tone for the final chorus. I added richer harmony, and I also tried using extended techniques such as falls, cup mutes, flutter-tonguing and trombone glissandi. Not every idea worked.

Overall, I think the arrangement is successful, because the song stays recognisable while the band’s full range of timbres is used. If I developed it further, I would want to hear it played live to check the balance and whether players have enough time for the mute changes.

I learned that arranging depends on careful listening and editing, not on adding as many ideas as possible. I did overwork it at times, but I often came back to the original. Often the simpler chord is the better one.

item.title: Research Task 3: Modern Ensembles
item.dc:creator: Pedro
item.description: Comparing the Steve Martland Band and Orlando Gough’s ensemble Man Jumping reveals two different approaches to instrumentation in modern alternative ensembles. In the Steve Martland Band, the brass and reed instruments take on an aggressive, front-line role...
item.content:encoded:
Comparing the Steve Martland Band and Orlando Gough’s ensemble Man Jumping reveals two different approaches to instrumentation in modern alternative ensembles.

In the Steve Martland Band, the brass and reed instruments take on an aggressive, front-line role as the primary melodic engine. In Kick, the trumpet, saxophone, and trombone function together as a unified driving force rather than individual soloists. Martland places these instruments at the front of the texture, pairing them with different timbral partners across different pieces. In Principia, the brass is paired with violin, creating a sharp acoustic edge. In Terminal, Martland pairs the horns with electric guitar and saxophone, creating a punchy layer. The writing is repetitive and rhythmic, using the dynamic weight of the brass to maintain momentum and push the pulse forward.

In contrast, Orlando Gough uses brass in a more supportive and varied way. In World Service, the brass instruments do not dominate the ensemble as they do in Martland’s work. Instead,they appear punctually, sharing space with the rest of the instruments and adding brief colouristic accents. In The Big Swing, the brass sounds processed and electronic rather than purely acoustic, with only the solo saxophone retaining its natural acoustic tone. In In the Jungle, the solo saxophone is transformed through digital processing and heavy reverb, mimicking the timbre of an electric guitar.

These two approaches offer useful models for ensemble writing. The Steve Martland Band demonstrates how to deploy a brass section as an acoustic wall of sound within an electric-acoustic ensemble. Man Jumping shows how electronic transformation and reverb can blur the boundary between acoustic wind instruments and electronic timbres.

item.title: Exercise 2: Orchestral Brass – the Past and the Present
item.dc:creator: Pedro
item.description: In Bach the brass carries a distinct fanfare style. The high trumpets take centre stage to bring pomp, pushing their bright sound over the rest of the ensemble rather than staying in the background. Bach...
item.content:encoded:
In Bach the brass carries a distinct fanfare style. The high trumpets take centre stage to bring pomp, pushing their bright sound over the rest of the ensemble rather than staying in the background. Bach pairs the trumpets rhythmically with the timpani to accentuate strong metric beats, while using imitative passages with the woodwinds to vary the timbral balance. The harmony remains mostly consonant, with the brass reinforcing the tonal framework.

In the third movement of Mahler’s Symphony, the brass application changes. Mahler uses short, dissonant staccato bursts and a piercing trumpet sound that works in close relationship with the strings. The lower brass registers deliver deep fortissimo weight, creating a daring sound. The groups and harmonies on the brass occasionally carries an almost jazzy character. Solo trumpet lines cut through and Mahler frequently deploys sudden brass accents to mark key structural transitions or force the listener’s attention toward a change in thematic direction.

In Stockhausen’s Gruppen, the brass section is dismantled and rethought. In the opening section, short brass bursts are masked within the wider ensemble texture, adding spatial ambience rather than standing out as traditional foreground melodies. Later in the piece, extended techniques and various mutes alter the acoustic identities of the instruments. Rather than treating brass as a single unified section, Stockhausen distributes the brass instruments across three separate orchestras placed around the hall, turning brass sound into a pointillistic, multi-directional spatial element.

Comparing the three works reveals differences and similarities. The primary difference lies in function and texture. Bach treats brass as an emblem of ceremonial joy and harmonic clarity. Mahler pushes brass into aggressive contrapuntal tension. Stockhausen abandons traditional melody entirely, using muted brass for timbral shifts and spatial distribution.

Despite these differences, a core similarity remains. Across all three eras, composers rely on brass instruments for structural punctuation and dynamic power. Whether in Bach’s rhythmic pairing with timpani, Mahler’s fortissimo transition markers, or Stockhausen’s explosive burst, brass retains its capacity to define momentum and signal major structural shifts.

item.title: Exercise 1: Modern Brass Instruments
item.dc:creator: Pedro
item.description: George Enescu: Légende I expected a virtuosic showcase, but Légende turned out to be a subtle study in register and dynamic space. The trumpet moves from sustained notes in the low register up into the high register softly and beautifully. The...
item.content:encoded:
George Enescu: Légende 

I expected a virtuosic showcase, but Légende turned out to be a subtle study in register and dynamic space. The trumpet moves from sustained notes in the low register up into the high register softly and beautifully. The piano plays high notes when the trumpet is silent, which prevents the frequencies from clashing. In fast passages, the trumpet reaches a fantastic speed, almost like a buzzing bumblebee, while the dynamic range drops to a pp that is almost silent before bursting into a very strong and piercing ff. What struck me most was how intimate the trumpet sounds in its quiet upper register. High trumpet lines do not need heavy dynamics to carry well.

Peter Maxwell Davies: Sonata for Trumpet and Piano 

In this sonata, the piano and trumpet fight much more directly for attention. The lower registers of the trumpet turn a bit weaker when other sounds are present, but the higher it goes, the more it pierces through the piano. Even against heavy keyboard chords, the trumpet cuts through whenever it ascends into its highest register. In its lowest register, however, it loses projection and gets swallowed by the piano sound. When writing for the lower register of the trumpet, surrounding accompaniments must be kept thin, reserving the upper register for moments where the trumpet needs to lead over complex ensemble layers.

Susan Mutter: Ages

This work demonstrates four distinct sides of the trombone across its movements. In the first movement, the trombone is mellow, following the piano through middle and high registers. The second movement shows more strength and punchy accents, where the piano leaves space by playing mostly when the trombone is silent.What struck me most in the third movement was the speed and staccato, which push a strong rhythmic sound and turn the trombone into a percussion-like driver. The fourth movement is lyrical and beautiful, sounding almost like a soft trumpet in its higher register. Writing in the high tenor register offers an effective singing voice for solo brass passages.

Paul Hindemith: Sonata for Trombone and Piano

Hindemith pairs a strong trombone against an active piano part. The low register sounds very strong when played forte, keeping up with the heavy piano writing. The transition from rapid notes to long sustained ones works extremely well, and the speed between registers makes the sound feel anxious yet interesting. The rapid jumps between high and low registers generate constant dynamic tension.

Olivier Messiaen: Appel Interstellaire 

The sound of the French horn here feels rougher and more spatial than the clean edge of a trumpet or trombone. Messiaen uses the solo horn to explore extreme dynamic contrast. When muted, the sound effect is almost like a whisper, sounding distant and eerie. It can be scary and surprising when it pushes hard on the dynamics into unmuted fortissimo calls.

Ludwig van Beethoven: Horn Sonata in F major, Op. 17 

Beethoven presents a much more mellow sound than Messiaen, especially in piano and pianissimo passages, pairing singingly with the piano. The staccato works very well,particularly when rising through the registers. The low register almost sounds like another instrument, with a deep bass that is not rough like the higher register. The mid-register blends with the piano in a vocal, lyrical manner.

Øystein Baadsvik: Fnugg

This tuba can sound like two notes played at the same time, creating a didgeridoo-like drone sound. It is possible to hear the player singing into the instrument while playing low pedal tones, which produces an unexpected acoustic effect similar to a muffled electric guitar. Hearing vocal pitch layered over tuba resonance completely redefines the instrument, turning a heavy bass pipe into a complex rhythm generator.

Ralph Vaughan Williams: Concerto for Bass Tuba and Orchestra 

The lower register of the tuba is very deep and loud, but the higher registers work surprisingly well too. The tremolos sound very good, and fast melodic runs demonstrate unexpected agility. The lower register delivers expected depth, but the upper register carries a warm, expressive cantabile quality. The tuba is capable of fast notes, so it should not be restricted to simple bass notes on main beats.

item.title: Research Task 2: Brass Bands and Wind Bands
item.dc:creator: Pedro
item.description: Brass bands: instrumentation and style The British brass band has had a standard line-up since the end of the nineteenth century. It has 25 players plus percussion: nine B-flat cornets (four solo, two seconds, two...
item.content:encoded:
Brass bands: instrumentation and style

The British brass band has had a standard line-up since the end of the nineteenth century. It has 25 players plus percussion: nine B-flat cornets (four solo, two seconds, two thirds and one repiano), one E-flat soprano cornet, one flugel horn, three tenor horns, two baritones, two euphoniums, two E-flat basses, two B-flat basses, two tenor trombones and one bass trombone (Herbert, 1992). There are no woodwinds. Percussion was banned from contests for part of the twentieth century and came back in the 1960s (Herbert, 1992).

The style grew out of transcriptions. Herbert (1992) groups the repertoire into three types: classical music, especially Italian opera overtures and selections, popular dances such as quadrilles, schottisches and polkas, and functional pieces such as anthems, carols and folk tunes. Modern players are known for almost constant vibrato and crisp articulation (Herbert, 1992).

Wind bands: instrumentation and style

The wind band has no fixed line-up. Rhodes (2007) says that no common standard has ever been fully achieved, because band music differs from one country to the next. The ensemble can include flutes and piccolo, oboes, bassoons, a full family of clarinets from E-flat to contrabass, saxophones, cornets and trumpets, horns, trombones, euphoniums, tubas and percussion (Rhodes, 2007).

The balance changes by country. Rhodes (2007) quotes Revelli: Germany recommends one-third woodwinds, France and Italy one-half, England about one-half, and America two-thirds for concert bands. French and Italian bands use the full saxhorn family. British bands favour cornets over trumpets. American bands often use saxophones in place of bassoons.

Size changes too. Sousa’s band in 1892 had 14 B-flat clarinets, three saxophones and 29 players in the other sections. The University of Illinois band in 1938 had 24 B-flat clarinets and instruments such as the heckelphone and the sarrusophone (Rhodes, 2007). The wind ensemble, started by Frederick Fennell at Eastman in 1952, uses mostly one player per part to avoid heavy doubling (Rhodes, 2007).

The early wind band repertoire came mostly from orchestral literature (Rhodes, 2007). In the twentieth century composers wrote original works for the band. Rhodes mentions Holst’s Suite in E-flat, Grainger’s Lincolnshire Posy and Schuman’s George Washington Bridge.

Brass bands: history and development

Before the 1830s, bands of wind and string instruments played in rural Anglican churches. They declined in the 1830s, and bands that called themselves brass bands appeared (Herbert, 1992). Claims about the “first” brass band have no reliable evidence. In 1838 Robert Thompson Crawshay formed a band of 20 players at Cyfarthfa Castle, probably the first virtuoso British brass band (Herbert, 1992).

Herbert (1992) dates the movement to 1844. That year the Distin family gained the franchise to import Adolphe Sax’s valve instruments. Amateur playing increased and the first well-documented contest followed in 1845 at Burton Constable. Valve instruments were quick to learn and cheap to make. Cornopeans cost £5 to £10 around 1840 and new cornets cost about £3 in the 1850s. Besson made 52,000 instruments between 1862 and 1895 (Herbert, 1992).

Money and class both mattered. Middle-class reformers promoted music as a “rational recreation” and supplied instruments, repertoire and encouragement. Some industrialists sponsored bands. John Foster founded the Black Dyke Mills Band in 1855 for his mill workers (Herbert, 1992). Herbert argues that the idea of industrialists paying for everything is almost certainly untrue. Most bands raised money from subscriptions, concerts and contests, and hire purchase schemes helped them buy instruments. The working class gradually took control of the movement.

Contests shaped the sound. Railways and cheap excursion fares brought bandsmen from wide areas. The first Belle Vue contest in Manchester reportedly drew 24,000 people (Herbert, 1992). Contests led to standard playing styles and to a standard instrumentation. From the 1880s, three conductors, Edwin Swift, James Gladney and Alexander Owen, won most of the major prizes for about twenty years, and their line-up became the standard. Leading bands were semi-professional. The Besses o’ th’ Barn Band registered as a limited company in 1887 and toured the world (Herbert, 1992).

By 1900 brass bands had a clear identity, but they were set apart from mainstream British music. Herbert calls this a “cultural ghetto”. Their lasting influence is on players, since many of the best British orchestral brass players of the twentieth century began in brass bands (Herbert, 1992).

References

Herbert, T. (1992) ‘Victorian brass bands: the establishment of a “working class musical tradition”’, Historic Brass Society Journal pp. 1-11.

Rhodes, S.L. (2007) ‘Instrumentation’, in A history of the wind band. Available at: https://windbandhistory.neocities.org/index-2 (Accessed: 11 October 2026).

item.title: Exercise 3: Big Band Style
item.dc:creator: Pedro
item.description: Antiphonal writing Syncopation Rhythmic feel Parallel movement within sections Extended chords
item.content:encoded:
Antiphonal writing

  • Bar 1: the saxes play first. The trumpets and trombones 1 and 2 answer with an off-beat hit, and all four trombones follow with tied quavers.
  • Bar 3: the altos play first, then the tenors and baritone answer. The trombones then take over with a rising triplet run while the saxes and trumpets rest.
  • Bar 4: the muted trumpets play on beats 1 and 2. The trombones answer with an off-beat chord and tied quavers, and the saxes close the bar.

Syncopation

  • Bars 1 and 2: the trumpets and trombones 1 and 2 hit off the beat. The altos play a short pickup at the end of each bar.
  • Bar 4: the trombones play an accent on beat 1, then a rest, then an off-beat staccato chord, then tied quavers.
  • The piano plays chords off the beat and ties them over, in all four bars.

Rhythmic feel

  • The saxes, trombones and muted trumpets all play triplet quavers.
  • In bar 4 the bass plays a triplet figure with a chromatic note.

Parallel movement within sections

  • Bar 1: all five saxes play the same rhythm.
  • Bar 3: the altos move together, and the tenors and baritone move together. All four trombones play the same rising triplet run.

Extended chords

  • The guitar plays stacked chords. The piano doubles them in both hands. This points to sevenths or ninths, but with the image quality is hard to name them.

item.title: Research Task 1: Brass Profiles
item.dc:creator: Pedro
item.description: Quick-Reference Sheets: Brass Instruments Trumpet Family French Horn Family Trombone Family Tuba Family Research The Trombone 1. History and Evolution The trombone traces its lineage back to the 15th-century development of the slide trumpet. Originally...
item.content:encoded:
Quick-Reference Sheets: Brass Instruments

Trumpet Family

  • Instruments: B♭ Trumpet, C Trumpet, D/E♭ Trumpet, Bass Trumpet, Piccolo Trumpet.
  • Range: Spans roughly from F♯3 (or F3 with extended bottom valve tubing) up to C6 and beyond for expert players (written pitch for B♭ trumpet). Divided into three functional registers: low register (dark, robust, but soft in volume), middle register (brilliant, clear, and resonant), and high register (piercing, highly projecting, and demanding of high physical endurance).
  • Timbre: Brilliant, commanding, heroic, and incisive. It easily penetrates dense orchestral tutti textures. Played softly, it offers a noble, warm singing quality; played loudly, it develops a brassy, metallic core edge.
  • Technique: Utilizes three piston or rotary valves to alter tubing length. Rapid articulation is achieved via single, double, and triple tonguing. A wide array of mutes (straight, cup, harmon, plunger, bucket) transforms its color, projection, and character.
  • Effective Usage: Primarily carries primary melodic lines, heroic fanfare motifs, and dramatic climaxes. Frequently doubles woodwinds or strings for textural reinforcement. Muted trumpet can evoke a distant, metallic, or jazzy atmosphere.

French Horn Family

  • Instruments: Double Horn in F/B♭ (the modern orchestral standard), Single Horn in F or B♭.
  • Range: Exceptionally wide range spanning from B1 (or lower pedal tones) up to F5/G5 (written in F, sounding a perfect fifth lower). Lower register is rich and solemn; middle register is warm, velvety, and lyrical; high register is bright, tense, and requires extreme embouchure control.
  • Timbre: Warm, mellow, noble, and deeply expressive. It possesses a unique acoustic capability to blend seamlessly with both woodwinds (acting as a tonal bridge) and brass. Can produce a harsh, brilliant brassy snarl when stopped (gestopft) or played brass-forte (cuivré).
  • Technique: Right hand is placed inside the bell, influencing intonation, timbre, and pitch by a semitone. Valves and the thumb valve (F/B♭ switch) alter tubing. Employs hand-stopping, transposing mutes, and cuivré timbral effects.
  • Effective Usage: Essential for lyrical solos, pastoral/hunting calls, rich harmonic pads, and unifying woodwind and brass choirs. Fundamental in chamber music (especially wind quintets) and symphonic writing.

Trombone Family

  • Instruments: Tenor Trombone (with or without F attachment), Bass Trombone, Alto Trombone (revived in classical and early music performance).
  • Range: Tenor trombone spans from E2 (extended down to B♭1 via F-attachment and pedal tones) up to F5. Notated in concert pitch, traditionally using tenor, alto, and bass clefs in classical orchestration, or bass clef in modern settings.
  • Timbre: Noble, powerful, resonant, and vocal. Ranges from solemn and majestic in chorales to aggressive, brassy snarls in fortissimo passages. Bass trombone provides a dark, massive acoustic anchor.
  • Technique: Uses a telescoping slide across seven primary positions, enabling continuous frequency sweeps (glissando) and precise microtonal intonation. F-attachment expands the lower register and provides alternate slide positions. Mutes (straight, cup, harmon) modify color.
  • Effective Usage: Forms the core harmonic backbone of the brass section, drives massive orchestral climaxes, and delivers solemn chorales. Tenor solos offer a rich tenor-vocal warmth; bass trombone anchors the brass bassline.

Tuba Family

  • Instruments: Bass Tuba (in F or E♭), Contrabass Tuba (in C or B♭), Euphonium / Tenor Tuba.
  • Range: Deep bass register, spanning from D1 (with pedal tones down to C1/B♭0) up to C4/E♭4. Non-transposing, notated in bass clef at concert pitch.
  • Timbre: Deep, velvety, round, and warm. At low dynamics, it provides a solid acoustic floor without masking other instruments; at high dynamics, it produces a powerful, room-shaking acoustic foundation.
  • Technique: Uses 4 to 6 piston or rotary valves to navigate expansive tubing and correct intonation quirks. Demands immense breath support. Rapid passages require clean articulation due to the large column of air.
  • Effective Usage: The absolute bass foundation of the brass section and the full orchestra. Supports low harmonies, doubles bassoons, contrabassoons, or string contrabasses. Capable of surprising agility and warm lyrical solo work.

Research The Trombone

1. History and Evolution

The trombone traces its lineage back to the 15th-century development of the slide trumpet. Originally known as the sackbut (derived from the Old French saqueboute, meaning “pull-push”), the instrument remained consistent in design from the Renaissance through the Baroque era. Compared to modern orchestral trombones, Renaissance and Baroque sackbuts featured significantly narrower bores, smaller bells, and thinner brass walls. This construction produced a delicate, agile, and vocal tone that blended effortlessly with human voices and early string/wind consorts, making it a cornerstone of sacred polyphony, civic wind bands, and Venetian polychoral music (such as the works of Giovanni Gabrieli and Heinrich Schütz).

By the late 18th and early 19th centuries, the sackbut evolved into the modern trombone, expanding in bell diameter and bore size to project within growing symphonic spaces. Introduced into the classical orchestra by pioneers like Christoph Willibald Gluck and Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart (notably in Die Zauberflöte and the Requiem), the trombone transitioned from a sacred/ceremonial instrument into a dramatic symphonic voice. Beethoven famously cemented its orchestral status in his Fifth, Sixth, and Ninth Symphonies, treating it as an embodiment of solemnity, divine intervention, and triumph. Throughout the Romantic era, the trombone section expanded from a classical trio (alto, tenor, bass) into three matching tenor/bass instruments or a standardized section of two tenors and one bass. The 20th century saw the widespread adoption of the F-attachment (invented in the 19th century by German makers), which added a rotary valve to bridge the physical gap between first and sixth/seventh slide positions, effectively extending the lower register and facilitating smoother execution of complex orchestral parts.

2. Repertoire Overview

  • Classical and Romantic Orchestral Milestones:
    • Mozart – Requiem (Tuba Mirum trombone solo)
    • Beethoven – Symphony No. 5 & No. 9
    • Berlioz – Symphonie Fantastique (Dies Irae statement)
    • Brahms – Symphonies No. 1, 2, 4
    • Mahler – Symphonies (frequently utilizing the trombone section for apocalyptic climaxes and chorales)
  • Concerted and Solo Repertoire:
    • Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov – Concerto for Trombone (1877, one of the earliest solo works)
    • Ferdinand David – Concertino for Trombone, Op. 4 (a staple of the Romantic training repertoire)
    • 20th-century contributions by Gordon Jacob, Henri Tomasi, Paul Creston, and contemporary works by composers like James MacMillan and Christopher Rouse.
  • Jazz and Big Band Evolution:
    • From early New Orleans jazz (Kid Ory utilizing the tailgate trombone style) to the sophisticated swing era virtuosity of Tommy Dorsey and Glenn Miller, and the bebop/modern jazz mastery of J.J. Johnson and Carl Fontana, who elevated the trombone to a nimble, lightning-fast solo instrument.

3. Playing Techniques: Conventional vs. Extended

Conventional Techniques

  • Slide Positions and Harmonic Series: The trombone divides its acoustic range into seven discrete slide positions, each lowering the fundamental harmonic series by a semitone.
  • Legato Tonguing (Doulx): Because the trombone does not rely on valves for every note change, changing notes within the same harmonic series requires a delicate articulation technique (ta-du or da-du) combined with precise slide movement to avoid unwanted glissandi between notes.
  • Pedal Tones: Playing below the standard fundamental of the first position by relaxing the embouchure to produce ultra-low foundational notes (used heavily in late Romantic and cinematic orchestration for dark, menacing timbres).
  • Vibrato: Traditionally achieved via lip/embouchure oscillation in classical playing, or slide vibrato (gentle manual pulsing of the slide) in early jazz and commercial styles.

Extended Techniques and Historical Shifts

Over the 20th and 21st centuries, contemporary composers and performers (such as Vinko Globokar, Luciano Berio, and Stuart Dempster) radically expanded the trombone’s vocabulary:

  • The Glissando: While historically used sparingly for comic or dramatic effect (e.g., in Ravel’s Boléro or Richard Strauss’s tone poems), the continuous glissando became a foundational structural element in avant-garde and contemporary concert music, exploiting the seamless transition of the slide across multiple positions.
  • Multiphonics: The technique of sustaining a pitched buzz with the lips while simultaneously humming or singing a different pitch into the instrument. This creates complex acoustic difference tones, chordal intervals, and aggressive growling effects.
  • Microtonality: Utilizing fractional slide positions (micro-intervals between standard positions) to produce microtonal scales, quarter-tones, and fluid pitch bends, explored extensively in spectral and modern concert music.
  • Mute Innovations: Beyond traditional straight, cup, and harmon mutes, contemporary playing incorporates plunger mutes, bucket mutes, velvet mutes, and “megafones,” as well as playing directly into piano strings with the sustain pedal depressed to create sympathetic resonance.
  • Air Sounds, Jet Whistles, and Slap Tonguing: Producing unpitched white noise (blowing air through the instrument without lip vibration), rapid percussive tongue slaps, and key/valve clicks, transforming the trombone into a percussion-adjacent and noise-inclusive sound generator.

  • Britannica, T. Editors of Encyclopaedia (2026). Brass instrument. Encyclopædia Britannica. https://www.britannica.com/art/brass-instrument
  • Hansen Media (n.d.). The Brass Section: Effects and Mutes. Orchestration Course. https://hansenmedia.net/courses/orchestration/lessons/the-brass-section-effects-and-mutes/
  • Hugill, A. (n.d.). The Orchestra: A User’s Manual – Trumpet & Trombone. https://andrewhugill.com/OrchestraManual/
